Iconic ‘90s Burger Yacht Sold for Less Than the Cost of Its Midlife Restoration
24 photos
Photo: IYC
A yacht can have several lives, and that always depends on how well its owners treat it. This 1998 raised pilothouse yacht from one of the greatest American yacht builders of all time is still a collector’s item, even though its newest owner grabbed it at a bargain price.
Less than a year ago, Silver Seas was marketed at almost $6 million; this month, it sold for less than $5 million. Sadly, as enormous megayachts and new-generation superyachts with all kinds of innovation, including those related to cleaner propulsion, take center stage, the ‘80s and ‘90s yachts being to look outdated and simply not big enough for the needs (and ego) of contemporary millionaires.
However, a yacht like Silver Seas will always have its fair share of admiration , no matter what, simply because it’s a Burger, and this all-American brand has earned a loyal following. Silver Seas is particularly interesting for yachting connoisseurs in general, and Burger followers especially, for being the largest open flybridge Burger designed by the legendary Don O’Keeffe in operation.
At the time of its delivery, in the Fall of 1998, it was officially the largest Burger ever built. The 107-footer (32.7 meters) may seem small by today’s superyacht standards, but it was a considerable upgrade for its owners at the time, who eventually moved on to an even bigger yacht from the same builder.
Photo: IYC Those famous original owners were none other than Tom and Grace Benson, owners of the NFL New Orleans Saints football team. Having previously owned and enjoyed a smaller, 88-foot Burger named Lady Grace (in honor of Grace Benson), they felt ready to upgrade to a bigger, more comfortable version, which would be named Lady Grace Marie.
Tom Benson was one of those serial yacht owners who stay faithful to a particular brand, and he even compared Burger yachts to Mercedes Benz cars, in terms of how both brands are able to deliver a proven DNA and still make continuous upgrades.
The new 107-foot Burger had a spectacular life ahead, as the Benson’s pleasure craft. It would travel to the Bahamas and Caribbean, return to New Orleans for the football season, and then cruise to Rockport (the Benson’s vacation town), and to Maine, during the summer.
The NFL boss had specific requirements for his bigger yacht, such as ample side decks, a bigger aft deck, and the engine room moved aft. Style-wise, the owners (Mrs. Grace in particular) envisioned an interior that would reflect the extensive time they had spent in Asia. They worked closely with Douglas Richey, the in-house interior designer for Burger at the time, to create an interior with clear Far East influences, but still classic in a timeless way.
Photo: IYC Shoji panels, tumbled limestone tile, and etched glass were defining elements of the original Lady Grace Marie’s aesthetic, before Japanese-style superyacht interiors became trendy. The Japanese “Shu” symbol, translated as “Welcome”, was seen everywhere onboard Lady Grace Marie.
Aside from the beautiful Japanese-inspired interior design, Lady Grace Marie sported significant engineering upgrades that made it one of the top luxury yachts launched in 1998. Things like a hydraulic passerelle, an Atlas Shorepower conversion system, and stainless steel fuel piping with swagelock fittings throughout, were premium innovations for the industry at that time.
Eventually, the Bensons moved on to their third Burger yacht, a 122-footer, while Lady Grace Marie was reportedly sold to a media publisher. The third and the fourth owners were both Burger Yacht connoisseurs. The fourth one, who renamed the 1998 yacht Silver Seas, as it’s known today, was the one who changed its destiny by investing wholeheartedly in a major refit, something that few yacht owners are generally willing to do,
At the time, Silver Seas had already two decades of cruising under its belt, and a comprehensive refit was needed for sure. The operation took several years, and some experts in the industry considered more of a reconstruction than a standard refit. The hull was refaired before the full paint job, all windows were reinstalled, all the interior woodwork was refreshed with new varnish, and new marble tile was installed throughout.
Photo: IYC A major overhaul of both engines was one of the most important parts of the refit, along with the addition of new electronics, new premium appliances for the galley, new carpeting, flooring, and water toys. Practically, almost everything was brand-new, ensuring a prosperous future for the late ‘90s yacht. Although this was a multi-million-dollar investment for the owner (added to what he had paid for the yacht itself), the newly-upgraded Silver Seas was never expensive.
When it was still valued at almost $6 million, brokers said that this was one-third of the reconstruction cost alone. This year, Silver Seas’ price dropped even lower, until it eventually found its new owner, someone who was lucky enough to get a beautiful 107-footer with the glorious Burger DNA and the condition of a brand-new yacht (meaning no more investments from his part would be needed).
Today, almost three decades after its famous debut, Silver Seas is still one of the finest examples of an American-built raised-pilothouse yacht below 50 meters. Tri-deck superyachts became almost ubiquitous in the 2000s, replacing the raised-pilothouse yachts of what is now a gone era.
As the name suggests, Silver Seas’ raised pilothouse sits several steps from the main level, boasting a spacious layout and expansive views, thanks to five canted windshields forward, plus two large windows on each side. Honey teak panels cover this classic pilothouse throughout, and generous seating allows guests to enjoy the view, without disturbing the helmsman.
Photo: IYC Technology-wise, this raised pilothouse provides upgraded navigation systems for safer and more comfortable cruising, including a couple of proprietary Burger systems for multiple function monitoring, and a night-vision camera.
In terms of accommodation, this 107-footer welcomes up to eight guests across four elegant staterooms. The master suite is located forward, with easy access from the lower foyer, and all the three guest cabins are located to port. All have private en-suites, cedar closets, and individual temperature controls.
Twin MTU engines allows comfortable cruising 16 knots (with a maximum speed of 20 knots). Just like in its original days, this almost 30-year-old yacht is still well-appointed for comfortable, extended vacations in the Bahamas and the Caribbean – the favorite playgrounds of many US millionaires.
As the biggest Burger built before the 2000s era, and the only one today with an open flybridge and raised pilothouse, Silver Seas enjoys an iconic status (although not reflected in the modest $4.9 million price tag). Sold to a new owner, it will continue to operate under a different name, but with the same DNA and instantly recognizable pastel blue hull.
Photo: IYC Burger Yachts, founded in 1863 in Manitowoc, Wisconsin, is not only one of the most important names in America’s yacht-building history, but also one of the oldest yacht builders in the world.
To own any Burger yacht is something to be proud of, and we should all be especially thankful to owners like Silver Seas’ previous owner, who are willing and happy to pump money into a Burger yacht just to ensure it will stay in shape for many more decades – that is how the legend lives on.
